short: The US reserves the right to tax its citizens as if the treaty were not in force.
definition: Convention art. 1(4)(a) provides that, except as stated in art. 1(5), the treaty does not affect a state's taxation of its residents or, for the United States, its citizens. This is why the treaty does not stop the US taxing a citizen living in Japan, and why relief comes through the credit rather than through any reduction in US taxing rights. Art. 1(5) then lists the articles that survive, and art. 23 on relief from double taxation is among them.

short: Convention art. 23, which allocates who credits whom and survives the saving clause.
definition: Art. 23(2) obliges the US to credit Japanese tax paid by a citizen or resident. Art. 23(3) then handles the specific case of a US citizen resident in Japan: Japan credits only the tax the US could have imposed on a non-citizen Japanese resident, the US credits the Japanese tax after that, and the income is deemed to arise in Japan to the extent needed to make that credit work. Because art. 23 appears in the art. 1(5) exception list, it is available notwithstanding the saving clause.

short: Income the US would source domestically is deemed to arise in Japan, so the foreign tax credit limitation has room.
definition: Convention art. 23(3)(c) deems income to arise in Japan to the extent necessary to allow the US to grant the credit required by art. 23(3)(b). IRC section 904(d)(6) then applies the limitation separately with respect to each such re-sourced item, so it creates a per-item limitation rather than a single pooled basket. It matters most where US domestic sourcing falls short, for example where Japanese tax on a particular sale is under the 10% threshold in section 865(g)(2).

short: Convention art. 13, under which gains on ordinary securities are taxable only in the state of residence.
definition: Art. 13(7) provides that gains from alienating property other than the categories enumerated in the preceding paragraphs are taxable only in the state of which the alienator is a resident. Ordinary listed securities are not enumerated, so once the taxpayer is a Japanese resident, Japan holds the treaty taxing right over their portfolio gains. The saving clause lets the US tax them anyway, which is what makes art. 23 necessary.

short: Convention art. 4, which resolves dual residence through a cascade of tests.
definition: Where both states would treat an individual as resident, art. 4 resolves it in order: permanent home, centre of vital interests, habitual abode, nationality, and finally competent authority agreement. A US citizen living in Japan is generally a treaty resident of Japan. This matters for which state's treaty rights apply, though the saving clause limits what that achieves against US tax.

short: Form 8833, used to disclose a position taken under a tax treaty, with a penalty for failing to file.
definition: IRC section 6114 requires disclosure of treaty-based return positions, made on Form 8833, with a penalty for non-compliance. Whether re-sourcing under Convention art. 23(3) requires disclosure, and in what circumstances, is not established in this repository and should be confirmed before relying on the position.

short: A separate US-Japan agreement determining which country's social security system applies.
definition: Distinct from the income tax convention. It prevents dual social security coverage and determines which system a worker contributes to, evidenced by a certificate of coverage. Japanese social insurance premiums are not income taxes and so are not creditable under IRC section 901; whether they are deductible is not established here. The agreement itself is not yet archived in this repository.
